name: LP5912-3.3DRVR
title: 500 mA low-noise, low-quiescent-current LDO regulator
summary: The LP5912 is a fixed-output linear regulator for loads up to 500 mA, running from 1.6 V to 6.5 V with outputs from 0.8 V to 5.5 V. It is aimed at RF and analog loads: 12 µVRMS output noise with no bypass capacitor, 75 dB PSRR at 1 kHz, 30 µA quiescent current and 95 mV dropout at 500 mA for outputs of 3.3 V and up. It is stable with 1 µF ceramic capacitors on input and output, and adds an enable input, a delayed power-good output, output discharge, soft-start and protection against overcurrent, overtemperature and reverse current. It comes in a 2 mm × 2 mm 6-pin WSON with an exposed pad.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: The regulator with its two required ceramic capacitors: one from IN to ground, one from OUT to ground. EN is brought out as its own control input. PG is pulled up to the output through RPG, and that node is brought out as the power-good signal VPG. NC is left unconnected.

parts.note: input capacitor, ceramic, no more than 1 cm from IN
output capacitor, ceramic X5R or X7R, 1 µF to 10 µF, ESR 5 mΩ to 500 mΩ

notes: Some applications need more than 1 µF on the input or the output.
A PG pull-up of 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ works best.

where.TTOP: temperature at the centre of the package's top face
where.PD(MAX): maximum dissipation, from the allowed-dissipation equation

operation.text: Each LP5912 has a fixed output set at the factory. Outputs from 0.8 V to 5.5 V are possible in 25 mV steps; voltages not in the ordering table are made on request.

A PMOS pass device between IN and OUT is driven by an error amplifier that compares a bandgap reference with a resistor divider inside the part from OUT. Around it sit a current limit, reverse-current protection, soft-start that limits in-rush current, thermal shutdown, a 100 Ω output discharge switch, and the power-good comparator with a fixed 140 µs delay. The EN control block has a 3 MΩ pull-down to GND. No noise-bypass capacitor is needed.

EN is held low by its internal 3 MΩ resistor, so an open EN leaves the part off. Above VEN(ON) (1.3 V minimum) the regulator is fully on under all conditions; below VEN(OFF) (0.3 V maximum) it is fully off. When off, the output stage is disabled, PG is pulled low and the output discharge resistor is switched on.

With EN low, a pull-down of about 100 Ω from OUT to ground empties the output capacitor. If another supply holds OUT up while EN is low, that supply drives current into this resistor to ground; that current is discharge current, not reverse current.

A detector trips when VIN falls below VOUT. It turns the regulator off and disconnects the body diode of the PMOS pass device, so no current flows back from OUT to IN, for example when a large output capacitance holds OUT up as the input collapses. Reverse leakage IRO, taken at IN, is 10 µA typical, 150 µA maximum with VIN = VEN = 0 V and VOUT = 5.5 V.

Overloads and short circuits are met by a current limit, which is a protection, not a continuous operating mode. The limit holds the output current constant at ISC (700 mA to 1100 mA at 25 °C), so a falling load resistance pulls the output voltage down. With the output low and current at the limit, dissipation can be high enough for thermal shutdown to act.

At a junction temperature of about 160 °C the output is switched off; it comes back on near 145 °C. Under sustained high dissipation the part cycles on and off between these points, which caps its temperature and keeps it from damage.

PG is an open-drain output. It pulls low when VOUT drops below PGLTH (90 % of nominal, typical) and goes high impedance once VOUT climbs above PGHTH (94 %, typical); a pull-up resistor to an external supply turns it into a logic signal, and that supply has to give valid levels for the circuit reading it. A pull-up of 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ works best. The rising edge is delayed about 140 µs after VOUT passes PGHTH; a fall below PGLTH pulls PG low at once. The PG state is valid only with VIN at 1.6 V or more. When PG is unused, the pull-up can be omitted and PG tied to ground or left open.

There is no dedicated undervoltage lockout. The internal circuits are not fully working below VIN = 1.6 V, and the output is in regulation only once VIN is at least 1.6 V or VOUT + VDO, whichever is higher.

An internal soft-start limits the in-rush current while the output rises. At turn-on the output reaches 95 % of nominal about 200 µs after EN passes VEN(ON), with start-up overshoot of 5 % of nominal at most.

An input capacitor is needed for stability: at least 1 µF from IN to ground, no farther than 1 cm from IN, its ground going to a quiet analog ground. For good load-transient behaviour it should be at least as large as the output capacitor; more output than input capacitance is acceptable while the input has at least 1 µF. Ceramic, tantalum or film parts can be used, with no ESR requirement, but its tolerance and temperature drift have to keep it within 1 µF ±30 % over temperature. If ground impedance or input inductance cannot be kept low, or the source is reached through long leads, use 10 µF or more. A tantalum input capacitor fed from a low-impedance source such as a battery needs a surge-current rating confirmed by its maker.

A 1 µF ceramic is the intended output capacitor. Any X5R or X7R ceramic, 1 µF to 10 µF, with ESR from 5 mΩ to 500 mΩ suits it, connected from OUT with a good return to GND. The minimum capacitance and the ESR window are both stability requirements. Tantalum or film parts also work but cost more and take more room.

Between 1 µF and 10 µF ceramics are the smallest, cheapest and lowest-ESR choice, which also helps filter high-frequency noise; a typical 1 µF ceramic has 20 mΩ to 40 mΩ ESR, inside the stable range. X7R is preferred, holding its value within ±15 % over temperature. A tantalum capacitor with ESR in range is larger and dearer than the equivalent ceramic, and its ESR roughly doubles between 25 °C and –40 °C, so leave margin.

The required 1 µF output capacitor does not have to sit at the OUT pin: it can be 5 cm to 10 cm away, so capacitors already present on the load can serve. It must then be connected straight between OUT and GND with no vias. Keep wiring inductance low, below 35 nH: wide traces, the output trace layer next to the ground layer, no vias if possible and many in parallel if not. For fast load steps, use an input capacitance at least equal to the total capacitance on the output node.

The regulator dissipates the input-output difference times the load current. Running with the smallest headroom above dropout reduces dissipation and raises efficiency, while more headroom improves PSRR and transient response. In the WSON package most heat leaves through the exposed pad into the board, so the pad should connect through thermal vias to an inner ground plane with enough copper. RθJA depends strongly on the board's copper area, weight and plane layout; the published RθJA is measured on the JESD51-7 board and serves only to compare packages. On a well-designed board RθJA is RθJC(bot) plus the thermal resistance of the copper acting as a heat sink.

The ψJT and ψJB characterization parameters depend little on copper spreading area, so measured top-of-package or board temperatures give a practical estimate of junction temperature. They are not true thermal resistances.

The input supply runs from 1.6 V to 6.5 V and should be clean and tightly regulated. For full regulation and best dynamic behaviour it should sit 0.5 V or more above VOUT. It needs 1 µF or more placed no farther than 1 cm from IN.

PSRR, noise and transient response depend on the board layout, and a layout good enough for an ordinary regulator can spoil them. Mount both capacitors on the component side with the regulator, as close to it as practical, and return their grounds to the GND pin with short, wide copper. Avoid long or narrow traces and vias in these connections: their inductance and resistance hurt performance, most of all during transients.
Typical layout: COUT beside OUT (pin 1); CIN beside IN (pin 6), its ground end toward GND (pin 5); RPG beside PG (pin 3); two thermal vias in the exposed pad.
